common_name: Tricolor Iron Cross Begonia (Cream-Edged Variegated Sport of Begonia masoniana)

planting.note: Divide and pot rhizome sections in spring, keeping the rhizome sitting on top of a humus-rich, fast-draining mix rather than buried, and provide extra humidity to support the thinner variegated leaf tissue.

directions: This sport of the species Begonia masoniana keeps the raised, quilted leaf texture and dark brown iron-cross center of its parent but adds a wide, creamy-white band running out to the leaf margin, separated from the cross by a ring of green. Because the cream tissue carries less chlorophyll, give it slightly brighter indirect light and higher humidity than plain-leaved Iron Cross Begonia to avoid scorch and keep growth vigorous. Propagate by rhizome division rather than leaf cuttings when possible, since division more reliably preserves the variegated pattern. It is commonly grown in terrariums and enclosed cabinets where humidity stays consistently high.

common_name: Nigramarga Eyelash Begonia (Black-Patterned Miniature Rhizomatous Begonia)

planting.note: Divide rhizome clumps or root leaf cuttings in spring in a shallow pot of humus-rich, fast-draining mix; this miniature stays compact enough for terrariums and dish gardens.

directions: A darker-leaved botanical variety of the eyelash begonia, nigramarga bears tiny heart-shaped leaves so densely marked in near-black along the veins that the green base color is reduced to narrow highlights, with fine white bristles fringing the leaf edges like eyelashes. Small white to pale pink flowers rise just above the foliage, most freely in winter. Its slow, tidy, creeping rhizome and diminutive scale make it one of the most popular miniature begonias for enclosed terrariums and bonsai-style dish plantings. Let the soil surface dry slightly between waterings and keep it out of direct sun, which quickly bleaches the dark leaf pigment.

common_name: Bethlehem Star Begonia (Star-Centered Miniature Rhizomatous Begonia)

planting.note: Divide rhizome sections or root leaf cuttings in spring in a shallow container of humus-rich, fast-draining mix; this is among the smallest-leaved begonias and suits compact pots and terrariums.

directions: A compact cultivar of the eyelash begonia, Bethlehem Star carries small, almost black leaves centered with a bright, star-shaped flash of green, one of the most striking contrasts among the miniature rhizomatous begonias. White to light pink flowers appear above the foliage in spring. It keeps a neat, mounding shape without pinching and grows easily given bright indirect light with a little gentle morning sun, which helps intensify the leaf contrast. Allow the soil to dry somewhat between waterings, since the shallow rhizome is prone to rot in constantly soggy mix.

planting.note: Root leaf or rhizome-section cuttings in spring in a humus-rich, fast-draining mix; give it the same bright shade conditions as its parent, Beefsteak Begonia.

directions: This crested sport of Beefsteak Begonia produces thick, glossy, deep olive-green leaves with heavily ruffled, frilled margins that curl and pucker like a head of loose-leaf lettuce, with the characteristic red-brown undersides of its parent showing at the curled edges. Clusters of pink flowers rise on tall stalks above the foliage, mainly in spring. It tolerates lower humidity better than many rhizomatous begonias, making it a forgiving choice for average indoor rooms as well as shaded porches in frost-free climates. Keep it in bright shade or filtered light, since the crested leaf margins can scorch in direct sun, and propagate new plants readily from leaf or rhizome cuttings.
